claims.claim: Existentialism is a philosophy that starts from the single (first-person) individual
claims.evidence: SEP existentialism [intro] 'existentialism generally begins in medias res, amidst our own situated, first-person experience'

claims.claim: That individual must choose how to live
claims.evidence: SEP [4. Freedom] 'it is up to the individual to make his, her, or their own identity through choices and actions'; [4.1] 'I alone am answerable to whatever options I choose'

claims.claim: Existentialism is a loose family of ideas, not a tidy school
claims.evidence: SEP [intro] 'certainly not a reference to a coherent system or philosophical school'; 'a set of overlapping ideas that bind the movement together'

claims.claim: It starts from concrete first-person life rather than a detached 'view from nowhere'
claims.evidence: SEP [2. Engagement vs. Detachment] rejects the 'God's eye view' or 'view from nowhere'; 'a careful analysis of first-person experience, of the concrete, flesh and blood particulars of everyday life'

claims.claim: Core claim: no fixed nature is given, so we make ourselves through choices
claims.evidence: SEP [intro] Existence Precedes Essence: 'our essence is not given in advance ... burdened with the task of creating ourselves through our choices and actions'

claims.claim: We are responsible for who we become
claims.evidence: SEP [intro] Freedom: 'we are free and responsible for who we are and what we do'

claims.claim: Kierkegaard and Nietzsche laid the groundwork in the nineteenth century
claims.evidence: SEP [intro] 'the conceptual groundwork of the movement was laid much earlier in the nineteenth century by pioneers like Søren Kierkegaard and Friedrich Nietzsche'

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir made it famous in mid-twentieth-century France
claims.evidence: SEP [intro] movement 'exploded on the scene in mid-twentieth-century France'; 'the most popular voices of this movement were French, most notably Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir'

claims.claim: Sartre called existence precedes essence 'the first principle of existentialism'
claims.evidence: SEP [3. Existence Precedes Essence] 'This is, according to Sartre, “the first principle of existentialism”'

claims.claim: He adapted the idea from Heidegger
claims.evidence: SEP [3] 'initially introduced early on in Heidegger’s Being and Time ... Sartre will later repackage this line'

claims.claim: No built-in human nature decides who we are
claims.evidence: SEP [3] 'there is no pre-given or essential nature that determines us'

claims.claim: A person first 'turns up' and only afterwards defines himself, through choices as life unfolds
claims.evidence: SEP [3] 'man exists, turns up, appears on the scene, and, only afterwards, defines himself'; 'situated choices we make as our lives unfold'

claims.claim: Facts like body, desires and historical setting limit us; existentialists call this 'facticity'
claims.evidence: SEP [3] 'our givenness (or “facticity”) ... our embodiment and spatiality, our creaturely appetites and desires, and the socio-historical context'

claims.claim: We can question those facts, give them meaning and decide what to do with them; that power is 'transcendence'
claims.evidence: SEP [3] 'capacity to rise above or “transcend” these facts'; 'surpass our facticity by calling it into question, interpreting it ..., and making decisions about how to deal with it'

claims.claim: What authenticity looks like varies across thinkers
claims.evidence: SEP sections 5.2-5.5 give distinct accounts per thinker

claims.claim: For Kierkegaard it is a passionate commitment that pulls a scattered life together
claims.evidence: SEP [5.2] 'a passionate, “personality defining” ... decision or commitment that binds together and unifies the fragmented and disjointed moments of our life'; life otherwise 'scattered and disjointed'

claims.claim: For Nietzsche it is saying yes to one's whole life, even to living it again forever
claims.evidence: SEP [5.3] 'The Overman is a “yes-sayer” who affirms every aspect of his life'; eternal recurrence: 'live the same life ... over and over for eternity'

claims.claim: For Heidegger it is 'resoluteness', a focused grip on one's possibilities that stays open to letting them go
claims.evidence: SEP [5.4] 'resoluteness ... giving life a sense of cohesion and focus'; 'I must also be willing to let go or give up on them'

claims.claim: For Sartre and Beauvoir it is clear-eyed acceptance of our unstable situation and responsibility for what we do
claims.evidence: SEP [5.5] 'a clear-eyed awareness and acceptance of the instability and ambiguity of the human condition ... to take responsibility'; 'to be concerned with what I do'

claims.claim: Existentialism is not only atheist
claims.evidence: SEP [intro] 'one finds secular and religious existentialists'

claims.claim: Kierkegaard was a Christian
claims.evidence: SEP [5.2] 'As a religious existentialist, Kierkegaard contends that this is what is required to enter the sphere of faith and become a Christian'
claims.note: Entailed rather than stated outright; acceptable.

claims.claim: Kierkegaard prized 'a truth which is true for me', lived and felt rather than proved
claims.evidence: SEP [2.1] 'it discloses “a truth which is true for me”'; 'cannot be reasoned about or explained logically'; 'felt rather than known'

claims.claim: In Fear and Trembling, God tells Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac
claims.evidence: SEP [5.2] 'In Fear and Trembling ... when God demands that he break this commandment and kill Isaac'

claims.claim: Abraham becomes a 'knight of faith' by leaping into a paradox reason cannot explain
claims.evidence: SEP [5.2] 'Abraham becomes a “knight of faith” by “leaping” (springer) into a paradox'; 'a truth that is fundamentally irrational and absurd'

claims.claim: He is alone with a choice no one else understands
claims.evidence: SEP [5.2] 'accompanied by anxiety and loneliness'; 'a path that no one else may understand'; 'cannot make himself understood to anyone'

claims.claim: The Jewish existentialist Martin Buber stressed meeting another person as a 'You', not an 'It'
claims.evidence: SEP [6.2] 'The Jewish existentialist Martin Buber ... I-It ... we become vulnerable to the other, not as an “it” but as a “you”'

claims.claim: Nietzsche and Sartre saw God as irrelevant or harmful to our deepest choices
claims.evidence: IEP [b. Anxiety and Authenticity] 'the existence of a transcendent deity is not relevant to (or is positively detrimental to) such decisions (a view broadly shared by Nietzsche and Sartre)'

claims.claim: Who counts as an existentialist is disputed
claims.evidence: IEP [intro] term is a 'catch-all'; IEP [f. Camus] 'every attempt to classify him a rather risky operation'; IEP [c. Heidegger] poses whether he can be classed as existentialist

claims.claim: The term names no single doctrine
claims.evidence: SEP [intro] 'there is no unifying doctrine'

claims.claim: Most thinkers grouped under it never used it or rejected it
claims.evidence: IEP [intro] 'most of the philosophers conventionally grouped under this heading either never used, or actively disavowed, the term'

claims.claim: Only Sartre and Beauvoir openly claimed it
claims.evidence: SEP [intro] 'only Sartre and Beauvoir explicitly self-identified as “existentialists”'

claims.claim: Heidegger repudiated Sartre's existentialism in his 'Letter on Humanism' (1947)
claims.evidence: IEP [c. Heidegger] 'in 1947 is published in a book form with the title ‘Letter on Humanism’. There he repudiates any possible connection of his philosophy with the existentialism of Sartre'

claims.claim: Both encyclopedias still count Heidegger among its key figures
claims.evidence: IEP [c. Heidegger] 'Heidegger can be classified as an existentialist thinker'; SEP [intro] lists Heidegger among those who laid the movement's conceptual groundwork
claims.note: SEP support is from the cited intro (groundwork list); 'key figures' is a fair paraphrase, borderline on SEP's side.

claims.claim: Camus gave a 1945 interview titled, in English, 'No, I am not an existentialist'
claims.evidence: IEP [f. Camus] '“Non, je ne suis pas existentialist” is the title of a famous interview ... 15 of November, 1945'

claims.claim: The SEP places his Myth of Sisyphus squarely in the existentialist tradition
claims.evidence: SEP Camus [1.] 'This essay belongs squarely in the philosophical tradition of existentialism but Camus denied being an existentialist'

claims.claim: Being and Nothingness is by Jean-Paul Sartre, 1943
claims.evidence: SEP Sartre [4.1] 'Being and Nothingness (1943)'

claims.claim: It is the movement's defining treatise
claims.evidence: SEP Sartre [4.1] 'remains the defining treatise of the existentialist “movement”, along with works from de Beauvoir'
claims.note: Source adds 'along with works from de Beauvoir'; dropping it is a minor simplification, not drift.

claims.claim: It covers radical freedom
claims.evidence: SEP Sartre [4.1] 'this quite radical philosophy of freedom'; 'radical human freedom'

claims.claim: It covers bad faith
claims.evidence: SEP Sartre [4.2] 'the chapter on bad faith in Being and Nothingness'

claims.claim: It covers the look
claims.evidence: SEP Sartre [4.3] 'In Being and Nothingness ... his descriptions of being subject to the look of another'

claims.claim: Existentialists were accused of neglecting social and political structures, with dangerous results
claims.evidence: IEP [b. Philosophy] 'Heidegger and the existentialist were also taken to task for paying insufficient attention to social and political structures or values, with dangerous results'

claims.claim: Heidegger remains notorious for his involvement with National Socialism
claims.evidence: IEP [c. Heidegger] 'He remains notorious for his involvement with National Socialism in the 1930s'

claims.claim: Nietzsche's ideal of the self-creating individual is openly elitist and anti-democratic
claims.evidence: SEP [5.3] Overman as figure of 'self-creation'; 'his account of authenticity is unapologetically elitist and anti-democratic'

claims.claim: Nazi ideologues exploited his work, in a way the IEP calls 'utterly misdirected'
claims.evidence: IEP [b. Nietzsche] 'The exploitation of his teaching by the Nazi ideologues ..., although utterly misdirected'

claims.claim: Camus accused Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Heidegger of escaping into 'forced hope'
claims.evidence: SEP Camus [3.3] Myth of Sisyphus 'written against existentialists such as Shestov, Kierkegaard, Jaspers, and Heidegger'; 'he rejects what he sees as their ultimate escapism'; 'That forced hope is religious in all of them'

claims.claim: Some argue the label does more harm than good, lumping very different ideas together
claims.evidence: IEP [intro] 'the term – insofar as it leads us to ignore what is distinctive ... and to conflate together significantly different ideas – does more harm than good'
